paper_title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) (Radford et al., 2018, 2019; Touvron et al., 2023) are increasingly being adopted as agents for automated AI research (AutoResearch) (Karpathy, 2026), where they pro1 Figure 1: Overview of automated LM development. pose ideas, implement changes, and execute experiments (Si et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025). promising application is language-model development (LM development), where agents explore architectural, optimization, and training choices and measure their effects on model performance (Chi et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). These experiments generate feedback that could help LLMs learn how to improve language models. Developing this capability could accelerate model development and support progress toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Chi et al., 2026) (Fig. 1(a)). Despite these advances, deciding what to try, i.e., research judgment, remains bottleneck for LLM-based research agents. Agents can implement and execute complex experiments, yet still struggle to identify changes that yield meaningful improvements (Li et al., 2026; Si et al., 2026; Chi et al., 2026). In LM development, effective choices depend on the target model and its training configuration: change that benefits one setting may not benefit another. With expensive training experiments, selecting promising changes is essential to making effective use of limited experimental resources. We therefore ask: how can language models learn to make better model-improvement decisions and transfer this capability to new models and training configurations? natural way to improve research judgment is to learn from past experiments. Experimental records can inform an LLMs decisions through in-context learning (ICL) (Brown et al., 2020; Novikov et al., 2025; Si et al., 2026), and can also improve predictions of experimental outcomes and the selection of promising proposals (Wang et al., 2026b). This suggests using experimental knowledge as feedback for parameter learning to improve an LLMs proposal-generation capability beyond in-context learning. However, learning from this feedback raises two key challenges (Fig. 1(b)-(c)). First, how can we obtain cheap and scalable training feedback? Training LLMs with reinforcement learning (RL) to generate better proposals requires feedback on numerous sampled proposals. The most direct feedback comes from executing each proposal and measuring its outcome (Si et al., 2026), but this requires costly model-training runs. For example, training 486M-parameter model on 8B tokens takes approximately 45 B200 GPUhours. GRPO-style RL (Shao et al., 2024) setup with 100 updates, 32 training states per update, and 8 proposals per state would require 25,600 proposal evaluations. Executing these proposals at the same per-run cost would consume approximately 1,152,000 GPU-hours, costing over $16 million. This motivates low-cost surrogate feedback without executing every proposal. Second, how can we keep surrogate feedback reliable as learning progresses? Accurate predictions on past experiments do not ensure reliable feedback throughout training. As learning changes which proposals the LLM generates, the surrogate must evaluate proposals that its experimental records may not cover. RL may then favor overestimated proposals, increasing surrogate rewards without corresponding real gains (Gao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026). scalable learning approach must therefore keep its feedback grounded in real outcomes on the proposals the current LLM generates. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, framework that trains LLMs with RL to generate effective proposals for LM development. To obtain cheap and scalable training signals, we use frozen LLM as research world model (RWM) (Wang et al., 2026b) to predict experimental gains relative to reference configuration without executing proposals. Grounded in an initial set of real experimental records provided as in-context knowledge, the RWM supplies predicted gains for constructing RL rewards (Yu et al., 2026). To keep this feedback reliable as training progresses, we introduce on-policy calibration: we periodically execute subset of the current policys proposals that the RWM ranks highly and incorporate their measured outcomes into its in-context knowledge. This targets real execution at proposals favored by RL, where overestimation can misdirect learning, and helps maintain prediction reliability as LLMs proposals change. Our contributions are: (i) Method. We propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL using RWMbased rewards grounded in real records and calibrated through targeted real execution; (ii) Experiments. Extensive real-execution experiments on held-out environments show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform frontier models such as GPT-6-sol and surpass baselines leveraging past experimental records at lower data-generation cost; (iii) Analysis. We show that RWM-based feedback provides informative rankings of proposal gains, while on-policy calibration mitigates overestimation and largely preserves ranking quality as training progresses, unlike fixed-record RWM that eventually performs worse than random.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: AutoResearch with LLM Agents. AutoResearch aims to automate empirical AI research through iterative idea generation, experimental implementation, execution, and analysis. Early work shows LLM agents ability to generate research ideas and conduct end-to-end experiments (Baek et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2024; Weng et al., 2026), with benchmarks evaluating these capabilities in machine-learning engineering and AI R&D (Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2026). To improve research outcomes, some methods iterate on candidate solutions with execution feedback while keeping the underlying agent fixed (Jiang et al., 2025; Novikov et al., 2025; Karpathy, 2026). Others instead train the agent on execution feedback, for machine-learning engineering (Yang et al., 2026a) and LLM model development (Si et al., 2026). However, these methods rely on costly real execution to obtain training signals, limiting learning at scale. In contrast, we train LLMs with feedback from world model that predicts experimental outcomes, enabling scalable learning with fewer real executions. sections.content: In this section, we present LM2LM. We first formalize AutoResearch for LM development and motivate RL-based proposer training (Sec. 3.1). To provide scalable feedback, we use frozen LLM as research world model (RWM) to predict experimental gains without executing proposals, and use its predictions as RL rewards (Sec. 3.2). sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: In this section, we first compare LM2LM with baselines on proposal quality and data-generation cost (Sec. 4.2) and evaluate its generalization to an unseen model family (Sec. 4.3). We then conduct 5 ablation studies to understand the contribution of on-policy calibration (Sec. 4.4) and analyze why RWM feedback can guide RL and how calibration sustains it (Sec. 4.5). 4.1 Experimental Setup Environments. We construct language-model training environments spanning four autoregressive (AR) families: OLMo-3 (Olmo et al., 2025), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), NanoChat (Karpathy, 2025), and Marin (Hall et al., 2025); and four diffusion families: E2D2-SW, E2D2 (Arriola et al., 2026), MDM (Nie et al., 2025), and BD3LM (Arriola et al., 2025). Each task specifies model family, model size, training budget, and reference training recipe. Each experiment trains the target model from scratch. Further details are in Appendix C.1. Data Construction. We split the tasks into 40 training and 10 held-out tasks. We curate and execute 300 proposals from library of training-recipe mechanisms on the training tasks, yielding 300 experimental records. Of these, 100 serve as the initial records M0 of LM2LM, grounding the RWM. We construct initial RL training states = (e, h) with histories containing 08 records of task from M0, expanded during RL (Eq. (7)). For evaluation, we construct 60 AR and 18 diffusion heldout research states using only real experimental histories. More details are in Appendix C.2. Baselines. We compare LM2LM with training-free and fine-tuning-based methods. (i) Training-free proposers: We evaluate LM2LMs base model and frontier LLM (GPT-6-sol) in both zero-shot and in-context learning (ICL) settings. For ICL, we use the above 300 experimental records as in-context (ii) Fine-tuned proposers: SFT fineexamples. tunes the base model on 300 (state, proposal) pairs constructed from the same records, and RFT-Real applies rejection-sampling fine-tuning (Yuan et al., 2023), keeping only the pairs whose proposals have positive measured gains. Both use the same base model and builder as LM2LM. Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate proposers on held-out research states through real execution, with each proposer generating four proposals per state. We measure experimental gains using validation bits per byte (BPB) for AR models and negative log-likelihood (NLL) for diffusion models. We compare LM2LM with baselines on proposal quality across held-out research states, following the evaluation protocol in Sec. 4.1. Table 1 reports the results. We observe: (i) Past experimental experience helps, but how it is used matters. Case studies are in Appendix H. 4.5 In-depth Dissection of LM2LM We further analyze why RWM feedback can guide RL and how calibration keeps it reliable. For this analysis, we extend training from 96 to 128 steps with fourth calibration of LM2LM (236 real runs) and compare it with the static variant whose RWM keeps M0 throughout; each variant is scored by the RWM it is trained with. Why Can RWM Feedback Guide RL? We examine the alignment between RWM-predicted and real-execution feedback by measuring the cosine similarity of group-relative advantages and the within-state pairwise ranking accuracy over four executed proposals per held-out AR research state. As shown in Figs. 5(a) and (b), LM2LM maintains advantage cosine of 0.500.71 and pairwise accuracy of 0.610.69, above chance levels of 0 and 0.5. Since DAPO optimizes group-relative advantages, this indicates that the RWM provides informative relative feedback for policy optimization. How Does On-Policy Calibration Help? To understand the gains from calibration in Sec. 4.4, we examine how the feedback of the static variant evolves as RL changes the proposers outputs  (Fig. 5)  . We observe that (i) Calibration maintains reliable relative feedback. As shown in Fig. 5(a), the static RWMs advantage cosine declines from 0.69 at step 16 to 0.42 at step 128, so its predicted advantages become negatively aligned with real ones, whereas LM2LM keeps it positive. Likewise, its pairwise accuracy drops from 0.72 to 0.37, below chance (0.5), while LM2LM maintains 0.61 (Fig. 5(b)). We further observe that scoring the same LM2LM proposals with M0 instead of calibrated records lowers pairwise accuracy from 0.61 to 0.46 at step 96 (Appendix I.2). These results indicate that on-policy calibration keeps the predicted advantages that DAPO optimizes aligned with real ones. (ii) Calibration limits reward overestimation. As shown in Fig. 5(c), the predictedreal reward gap of the static RWM rises sharply after step 64, reaching about 2.0 at step 96, whereas LM2LMs gap stays below 1 and decreases from 0.85 at step 96 to 0.17 at step 128 after the fourth calibration. Thus, calibration also keeps predicted rewards close to real ones, mitigating reward overoptimization (Gao et al., 2023). For example, our case studies in Appendix I.3 show that the initial RWM overestimates NanoChat optimizer change (predicted +0.7 to +1.25 vs. real 1.46), so the static variant raises its share of NanoChat training proposals from 30% to 79% by step 64. In contrast, the first calibration of LM2LM adds its real outcomes to the records, and the share falls to 8%. More metrics and case studies are in Appendix I.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective proposals for LM development, using frozen LLM grounded in real experimental records as an RWM and keeping it reliable through on-policy calibration. Extensive experiments across autoregressive and diffusion LM environments show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform frontier models such as GPT-6-sol and achieve higher gains than baselines leveraging past experimental records at lower data-generation cost. Our analysis shows that RWM-based feedback provides informative rankings of proposal gains, while on-policy calibration mitigates reward overestimation and preserves ranking quality as training progresses. These findings highlight RWM-guided RL as promising paradigm for learning research judgment from experimental feedback, offering potential path toward RSI.

sections.title: 6 Limitations
sections.content: Our study focuses on proposal-level improvements in LM development rather than end-to-end research campaigns. Although the RWM provides informative rankings and substantially reduces the need for real execution during RL, its predictions remain imperfect, and on-policy calibration still requires limited number of additional model-training runs. Future work could extend our framework to broader research environments, including LM post-training, and evaluate its effectiveness in longer, end-to-end research campaigns.

sections.title: 7 Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work studies the use of LLMs to automate research on language-model development. Such systems may help reduce the cost of experimentation and accelerate scientific progress, but they also introduce risks, including unreliable experimental conclusions, increased computational resource consumption, and the potential misuse of automated model-improvement capabilities. Our framework evaluates proposals in controlled training environments and uses real experimental outcomes to calibrate surrogate feedback. Nevertheless, predicted rewards and experimental gains do not guarantee the safety or broader usefulness of proposed model changes. We therefore emphasize the importance of human oversight, independent evaluation, and appropriate safeguards when applying automated research systems to more capable models or higherstakes settings.

sections.title: A More Details of Related Works
sections.content: A.1 World Models for LLM Agents. world model predicts the consequences of an agents actions, enabling planning or learning without interacting with the real environment (Sutton, 1991; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2023). Recent work uses LLMs as world models for reasoning (Hao et al., 2023), web navigation (Chae et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2024), text-based simulation (Wang et al., 2024), and agent training in synthetic environments (Chen et al., 2026). In AutoResearch, concurrent work WMRL (Yang et al., 2026b) uses frozen LLM as the world model to predict execution outcomes as RL rewards and rescales them with monotone mapping fitted on real executions at every training step. In contrast, LM2LM uses frozen LLM as the world model that learns research knowledge from real experimental records in context (Wang et al., 2026b), and improves its predictions on the current policys proposals by adding the outcomes of few top-rated ones to these records. A.2 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs Reinforcement learning (RL) (Shao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026) has become an effective approach to improving LLM capabilities, particularly through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Lambert et al., 2025). Methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and DAPO (Yu et al., 2026) optimize LLM policies using group-relative feedback without learned value function. While RLVR typically relies on inexpensive verification, such as checking mathematical answers or executing code, LM development requires costly model-training experiments to measure proposal quality. Recent work applies RL to automated AI research using execution feedback (Yang et al., 2026a; Si et al., 2026), but obtaining rewards through real execution at every training step limits scalability. In contrast, LM2LM uses RWM-predicted experimental gains as RL rewards, while periodically calibrating the RWM with selected real executions to maintain feedback reliability. A.3 Self-Evolving LLMs and Agents Self-evolving methods improve model or agent with data or feedback it generates itself. One line trains LLMs on self-generated solutions that are filtered or rewarded by verifiers or by the model itself (Zelikman et al., 2022; Gulcehre et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024). Another line lets agents modify their own code, prompts, or workflows and keeps the changes that improve benchmark performance (Lin et al., 2026b; Yin et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026c,d). These methods rely on feedback that is cheap to obtain, such as answer checking, code execution, or benchmark scores. In LM development, measuring single proposal requires full model-training run. LM2LM addresses this setting by learning from RWM-predicted gains and calibrating the RWM with small number of real executions, and it targets the ability to improve LM development, which recursive self-improvement ultimately requires. It is recomputed at the start of each training segment and held fixed within the segment; for the first segment, MADe is estimated from RWM predictions on proposals of preliminary run. sections.title: C Environments and Data
sections.content: C.1 Model Families Each family shares an architecture, training-data distribution, and evaluation metric across its tasks. AR Families. 14 OLMo-3 (Olmo et al., 2025): OLMo-3 small models trained on samples of Dolma 3 and evaluated by mean bits per byte (BPB) across ten downstream tasks (ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, four MMLU subsets, HumanEval, MBPP, and MATH-500). Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025): The official Qwen3 architecture and tokenizer. Training data (Dolma 3) and evaluation (ten-task BPB) are shared with OLMo-3. NanoChat (Karpathy, depthparameterized transformers trained on ClimbMix and evaluated by BPB on held-out ClimbMix validation shard. 2025): Marin (Hall et al., 2025): Marin architectures with the same training data and evaluation as OLMo-3. Diffusion Families. All four families are trained on SlimPajama with 2,048-token context and evaluated by the negative log-likelihood of true tokens accumulated along the models greedy, mostconfident-first unmasking order, measured in nats per token. E2D2 (Arriola et al., 2026): an encoder-decoder masked diffusion model with clean-token encoder and cross-attention decoder for noisy tokens. Noise levels are sampled per block, yielding block-autoregressive modeling. E2D2-SW (Wang et al., 2026a): This is an E2D2 variant with token-causal encoder and decoder trained on packed sliding windows of blocks but evaluated on non-overlapping blocks. BD3LM (Arriola et al., 2025): block diffusion model using single network over concatenated clean and noisy sequences with block-structured attention. MDM (Nie et al., 2025): full-sequence bidirectional masked diffusion model with one noise level per sequence; it appears only among the training tasks and has no held-out task. sections.title: E Additional Implementation Details
sections.content: E.1 Models and Prompts. The proposers backbone is Qwen3.8-27B. The RWM, GPT-6-sol, is queried with single API request per proposal at high reasoning effort, without tools. The builder, GPT-6-astra, runs as Codex agent (OpenAI, 2025) (codex exec) at high reasoning effort. Tables 13, and 14 list the prompts of RWM, and builder, respectively. E.2 RL Training We use DAPO with asymmetric clipping (ϵlow = 0.2, ϵhigh = 0.28), token-level policy-gradient loss, and no KL or entropy regularization. For dynamic sampling, we sample 277 states and retain 256 per rollout; importance-sampling ratios are clipped at 2.0. Proposals are sampled at temperature 1.0 with maximum of 20,000 generated tokens. Each rollout is followed by eight policy updates with global batch size of 256. We use Adam (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98), weight decay 0.1, and an initial learning rate of 106, multiplied by 0.7 after each training segment. E.3 On-Policy Calibration The candidates Cu in Eq. (9) are the proposals sampled by the current proposer on training states whose outcomes are not yet in Mu; in practice, we spread the selected top-rated proposals across training tasks and states. Each selected proposal is executed once on its training task, and the three calibrations add B0 = 31, B1 = 38, and B2 = 31 records. Calibration outcomes enter only the RWM records, not the histories of training states. E.4 SFT and RFT-Real Each SFT pair uses records executed proposal as the target, and state of the records own task whose history contains 07 other records of that task from the 300 records, chosen to diversify histories across pairs. RFT-Real keeps the 114 pairs whose measured gain is positive (76 AR and 38 diffusion). sections.title: F Additional Main Results
sections.content: F.1 Per-Family Results Tables 7 and 8 break the results down by model family, and gains vary across families: LM2LM attains the highest Avg@4 and Best@4 on OLMo-3, Qwen3, E2D2, and BD3LM and the highest Best@4 on Marin, but falls behind GPT6-sol-ICL in Avg@4 on Marin and E2D2-SW and behind Base-ICL in Best@4 on E2D2-SW. Although its AR advantage is largest on Qwen3, LM2LM still achieves the highest AR Avg@4 and Best@4 when excluding Qwen3 (4.42 and 10.68, vs. at most 3.09 and 7.58). On NanoChat, headroom is limited: no method improves by more than about 2σe (Best@4 at most 1.23 103 BPB), and GPT-6-sol-ICL is the only method with positive Avg@4. These results show that LM2LM can bring smaller open-weight model to frontier-level performance in proposing effective LM improvements. F.2 Statistical Robustness We express experimental gains in units of taskspecific seed noise σe, defined as the standard deviation of the reference configurations validation loss over three runs. Table 9 reports Avg@4 and Best@4 in units of σe, the fraction of proposals with gains exceeding 2σe, and Avg@4 relative to the reference loss. On AR tasks, LM2LM achieves an Avg@4 of 7.29σe, compared with at most 4.91σe for the baselines. Moreover, 50.8% of its proposals exceed 2σe, compared with 22.5% for Base and 40.0% for GPT-6-sol-ICL, while its Avg@4 corresponds to 1.28% reduction in reference loss.
